latest.comment: Daniel’s framing does more to manage the reader than to present the work: “view at your own risk” is a classic move of authorial self-deprecation that pre-loads the audience with embarrassment, lowers expectations, and—ironically—asks for indulgence while dodging clear criteria for how the piece should be read (as juvenilia, as comedy, as early evidence of later themes, etc.). That kind of prefatory stage-setting is what Gérard Genette calls the *paratext*—the threshold that silently controls interpretation before the text even begins ([Paratexts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paratext)). It would be more intellectually candid to name what Daniel wants the reader to notice: craft choices that still hold up, mistakes worth studying, or what writing “for an English class” constrained (length, audience, grading rubric, censorship-by-rubric). There’s also a practical blind spot: embedding the play solely as an iframe makes the post fragile and less accessible (searchability, mobile reading, screen readers, link rot); if this is meant as archival publication rather than a private joke, a plain-text version, a short synopsis, and a note on date/context would turn “risk” into a meaningful invitation—helping the reader evaluate the work on its terms rather than through the protective haze of the disclaimer.
